extracted.intended_audience: research software developers submitting to JOSS; JOSS editors and reviewers; people interested in software peer review and scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and reviewer checklist for submitting, reviewing, and accepting short software articles to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS). Covers submission eligibility, required repository/artifact elements, documentation/tests, reviewer checks, and procedural steps for archival and DOI issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The software must be open source by the Open Source Initiative (OSI) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must be open source by the Open Source Initiative (OSI) definition (https://opensource.org).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The repository must include a plain-text LICENSE file and use an OSI-approved license. The software submitted to JOSS is required to be shared under an OSI-approved open-source license.

rubrics_metrics.name: The software must have a research application
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must have a research application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS focuses on research software; submissions should enable or materially support research workflows rather than being purely general-purpose utilities without research relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitter should be a major contributor
rubrics_metrics.description: The submitter should be a major contributor to the software they are submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the submitting author has the authority and knowledge to address review comments and make required changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant new contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should be a significant new contribution to the available open-source software that either enables some new research challenge(s) to be addressed or makes addressing research challenges significantly better (e.g., faster, easier, simpler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS expects submitted software to be more than a trivial wrapper or minor tweak; it should materially add capability or improve research practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-complete software
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should be feature-complete, i.e., it cannot be a partial solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS does not accept incomplete prototypes that lack core functionality required for their stated purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article content and length constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS articles are deliberately short and only include an abstract describing the high-level functionality of the software, a list of the authors of the software (with their affiliations), a list of key references, and a link to the software archive and software repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles must not include other content often found in software articles, such as API descriptions or novel research results; API details belong in the software documentation and domain results belong in domain journals. The article is an 'advertisement' pointing to the software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software must be archived with a persistent identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: After review, the submitting author must make a permanent archive of the software (including any changes made during review) with a service such as Zenodo or Figshare and post a link to the archive in the review thread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The archive link (DOI) is associated with the submission (e.g., via @whedon set <doi> as archive) and is required before final acceptance so the software is properly archived and citable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code snippets in JOSS articles are MIT-licensed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any code snippets included in JOSS articles are subject to the MIT license regardless of the license of the submitted software package under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors retain copyright of their JOSS article and articles are published under CC BY 4.0; code snippets embedded in articles have MIT licensing to allow reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest confirmation (reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the reviewer I confirm that I have read the JOSS conflict of interest policy and that there are no conflicts of interest for me to review this work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must explicitly confirm no conflicts before proceeding; this is an explicit checklist item in the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Conduct confirmation (authors and reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers must read and adhere to the JOSS Code of Conduct; reviewers confirm they will adhere to it during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both authors and reviewers must confirm adherence during submission and review respectively; JOSS adopted the Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Repository: Is the source code for this software available at the repository URL?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer checks that the repository URL provided resolves to the actual source code repository containing the project under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository license file
rubrics_metrics.description: License: Does the repository contain a plain-text LICENSE file with the contents of an OSI-approved software license?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plain-text LICENSE file in the repo is required and must contain the full license text of an OSI-approved license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release version matches repository release
rubrics_metrics.description: Version: Does the release version given match the GitHub release?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The release version stated in the submission metadata should correspond to a specific release/tag in the repository so the archived DOI maps to the correct code version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship: Has the submitting author made major contributions to the software?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers check that the submitter is legitimately an author/contributor and not a third-party submitting on behalf of others without proper contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation (functionality check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Installation: Does installation proceed as outlined in the documentation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should attempt installation following provided instructions to confirm the install process works and dependencies are correctly declared. Ideally installation uses automated package management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality confirmation (functional claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality: Have the functional claims of the software been confirmed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should verify that the software performs the features it claims, e.g., by running examples or tests demonstrating core functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance confirmation (performance claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance: Have any performance claims of the software been confirmed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the authors make performance-related claims (speed, scalability), reviewers should verify them where feasible or request evidence/examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of need (documentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of need: Do the authors clearly state what problems the software is designed to solve and who the target audience is?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appears both in repository documentation and in paper.md; the statement should make clear research relevance and intended user community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation instructions and dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Installation instructions: Is there a clearly-stated list of dependencies? Ideally these should be handled with an automated package management solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependencies should be explicit and installation reproducible; use of package managers or environment files is preferred to manual dependency lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Example usage: Do the authors include examples of how to use the software (ideally to solve real-world analysis problems)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples should demonstrate typical use-cases and help reviewers/users exercise the software to confirm functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality documentation (API/docs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality documentation: Is the core functionality of the software documented to a satisfactory level (e.g., API method documentation)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation should explain core interfaces, inputs/outputs, and behavior so users and reviewers can understand and use the software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated tests or verification steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tests: Are there automated tests or manual steps described so that the function of the software can be verified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of automated tests (and a test suite that can be run) is highly desirable; if tests are absent, reviewers should have reproducible manual verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community guidelines for contribution and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Community guidelines: Are there clear guidelines for third parties wishing to (1) contribute to the software, (2) report issues or problems with the software, and (3) seek support?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CONTRIBUTING.md, issue templates, and clear support channels help future contributors and indicate a healthy open-source project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper authors and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors: Does the paper.md file include a list of authors with their affiliations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The short JOSS article must list authors and their institutional affiliations as part of the article metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: statement of need (paper.md)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of need: Do the authors clearly state what problems the software is designed to solve and who the target audience is (in the paper.md file)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper.md abstract/statement should succinctly summarize the software's purpose and target users; this is central to the published article's role as software advertisement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: references include DOIs where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: References: Do all archival references that should have a DOI list one (e.g., papers, datasets, software)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure bibliographic references in paper.md include persistent identifiers (DOIs) where applicable for proper citation tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, public review via GitHub issues
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS conducts reviews on the joss-reviews GitHub repository using public GitHub issues where editors, reviewers, and authors interact openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review discussions are visible, allowing discoverability, community commenting, and faster iterative communication compared with traditional closed reviews. Review threads document the review and are used to record archive DOIs and final acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers must confirm COI and may be invited openly
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors generally identify one or more reviewers from a pool of volunteers based on provided programming language and/or domain expertise; reviewers must confirm conflict-of-interest and code-of-conduct adherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS leverages GitHub discoverability to invite reviewers via mentions; editors typically contact multiple potential reviewers and select based on expertise and availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review administrative check
rubrics_metrics.description: A routine check by a JOSS administrator creates a 'pre-review' issue before an editor is assigned and the main review issue is created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-review identifies basic suitability and prevents premature creation of review issues; it is a gate before assigning an editor and starting formal review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-track for rOpenSci-reviewed contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: For submissions of software that has already been reviewed under rOpenSci’s onboarding guidelines, JOSS does not perform further review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor-in-chief is alerted with a note linking to the rOpenSci onboarding issue and the submission can be fast-tracked to acceptance based on that prior review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance process and metadata deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an article is accepted, JOSS gives it a DOI, deposits its metadata in Crossref, and the article is published; the editor-in-chief (or tooling) compiles the article PDF and deposits Crossref metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currently some final steps are handled by the editor-in-chief via the Whedon RubyGem and Whedon-API bot; JOSS plans to automate these steps so editors/authors can request compilation and metadata deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS editorial principle: aim to accept after improvements rather than reject for major revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike other journals, JOSS does not reject articles requiring major revision; while not yet accepted, articles remain visible and under review until the authors make adequate changes (or withdraw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to improve software and accept most articles after iterative public review rather than use rejection as a mechanism.
